newsitem.title: FRANCE: FRENCH GRAIN HARVEST STUCK BUT WEATHER CLEARS.
newsitem.headline: FRENCH GRAIN HARVEST STUCK BUT WEATHER CLEARS.

text.p: The tail-end of three days of bad weather is keeping the grain harvest idle in northern France but storms have mostly moved south where wheat and barley have been cut, Meteo France said on Thursday.
Most of the big-yielding northern areas still to be harvested have been caught up in this week's storms, boosting fears among farmers over crop damage or quality losses.
But brighter weather reached into the Paris grain belt by late Thursday afternoon and the national weather service predicted more fine spells on Friday.

Traders said grain prices firmed after heavy rain during the night and, to a lesser extent, because of improved export prospects after the European Commission all but cleared a total of 472,000 tonnes of soft wheat for export.
Standard quality Rouen-deivered wheat gained about 10 francs a tonne to 880 francs for August onwards. The price has risen 20 francs a tonne over the week mainly because of storms.
For guarantees of better quality wheat traders reported premiums bringing prices up to at least 900 francs. Wheat of 220 Hagberg and 11 percent protein traded at 900 francs.
There was also talk of far higher premiums for individual classes of millng wheat but few prepared to guarantee them.
Fob Moselle soft wheat hit 900 francs for August to December and some who had pre-sold guaranteed quality wheat were looking around for cover at 910 francs.
Fob Creil was notionally at 810 francs for September to January and for standard quality, but there were no sellers.

Wet weather risks adding to a perceived surplus of feed wheat and worsening pre-germination in the fields. But it has also helped to split the market wider than usual with hefty premiums for milling wheat with guarantees, traders said.
The weather was having a negative impact on test weight in many locations, they added.
About half the harvest is finished in the Beauce grain belt area near Orleans.
North of the Seine the harvest is 10 to 40 percent complete. Unripe grain in the far northeast around Lille has more to gain from the rain and is seen less vulnerable to damage.
Traders also reported a north-south divide.

They said the market was stuck between suppliers south of Paris, who were refusing to sell just-harvested crops on hopes of further weather problems in the north, and millers delaying purchases in a gamble that northern crops would take off again.
Matif soft wheat futures were flat to five francs higher.
NOTE - French domestic grains are traded on a "July basis," reflecting their underlying value without twice-monthly carrying charges.
